identification.summary: Aqua Blizzard (formerly ACTINIUM, earlier DEV-0157) is what Microsoft calls the Russia-based actor that other vendors track as Gamaredon [S1][S2]. Microsoft describes it as an espionage and data-theft actor that mainly targets Ukrainian government, military, judiciary, law enforcement and non-profit organizations [S1][S2]. Its hallmarks are high-volume spearphishing, heavily obfuscated VBScript and PowerShell, self-extracting archives and LNK files, and fast-changing infrastructure [S1][S2]. Unit 42 named the group in 2017 and reported a shift from off-the-shelf tools to custom malware [S10]. ESET reports that the group was still very active in 2024 and 2025, running many spearphishing waves against Ukrainian government and military institutions [S8][S9].
identification.firstObserved: Active since at least mid-2013, per LookingGlass 'Operation Armageddon' [S11] and Unit 42 [S10]. Microsoft said in February 2022 that the group had been operating for 'almost a decade' [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Aqua Blizzard. It was ACTINIUM until April 2023 and DEV-0157 before that [S1]. Microsoft's profile lists Primitive Bear, ACTINIUM, SectorC08, Shuckworm, Gamaredon, UNC530 and Armageddon as other names [S2]. Unit 42 uses Trident Ursa [S5], and Symantec uses Shuckworm [S6]. The name 'Gamaredon' is an anagram of 'Armageddon', taken from LookingGlass's 2015 report [S10][S11]. Microsoft notes that Aqua Blizzard is distinct from DEV-0586 (Cadet Blizzard) [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as Gamaredon Group (G0047) [S12].

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation, Federal Security Service (FSB). The Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) says the group consists of officers of the FSB in Crimea, operates from Sevastopol and takes orders from the FSB Center for Information Security (Center 18) in Moscow [S3][S9].
attribution.confidence: The attribution to the FSB is a Ukrainian government attribution (SSU, November 2021) [S3]. Microsoft repeats the Ukrainian attribution and says it observed ACTINIUM 'operating out of Crimea'; it does not give its own confidence level [S1][S2]. ESET says it believes with high confidence that Gamaredon collaborates with Turla [S7]. LookingGlass said in 2015 that it was 'highly confident' that the SBU's claims of FSB involvement were accurate [S11].
attribution.basis: The SSU named five individuals and cited intercepted communications, including published recordings of phone calls between members [S3]. Microsoft's telemetry places operations in Crimea [S1]. Vendor technical reporting from Unit 42, Symantec and ESET describes consistent tooling and targeting [S5][S6][S8][S9]. In 2025 ESET found technical links to Turla, another FSB-linked actor, with Gamaredon tools used to restart or deploy Turla's Kazuar backdoor [S7].

objectives: Microsoft describes the objectives as espionage: exfiltrating sensitive information, maintaining access, and moving laterally into related organizations [S1][S2]. Since October 2021 Microsoft has seen a focus on organizations critical to emergency response, territorial security, and the coordination of international and humanitarian aid to Ukraine [S1]. Secondary coverage of Symantec's 2023 reporting says the material stolen from Ukrainian security, military and government bodies included casualty, engagement, air-strike, arsenal-inventory and training reports [S6]. ESET says the group probably gives Turla initial access to selected high-value machines [S7].

sectors: Emergency response, territorial security and humanitarian-aid coordination organizations [S1]
Energy: an attempted intrusion at a petroleum refining company in a NATO member state [S5]
Western government entity operating in Ukraine [S4]
regions: Ukraine, the primary and in 2024-2025 almost exclusive target [S1][S2][S8][S9]
NATO member states, occasionally: the August 2022 refinery attempt [S5] and the NATO-country targeting ESET describes in 2022-2023 [S13]
targeting.notes: ESET reports that in 2024 the group refocused exclusively on Ukrainian government institutions [S8], and that throughout 2025 it targeted only Ukrainian governmental and military institutions [S9]. Targeting outside Ukraine appears opportunistic or tied to Ukraine support, but this is inferred from limited cases [S4][S5].

capabilities.summary: The tradecraft is high-volume rather than sophisticated. Initial access comes through spearphishing with macro documents that use remote template injection, web bugs that track email opens, and lures impersonating legitimate bodies such as the WHO [S1]. Later waves used archives and XHTML files with HTML smuggling to deliver HTA downloaders [S9]. From late September 2025 the group exploited the WinRAR flaw CVE-2025-8088 to plant downloaders in the Startup folder [S9]. Execution relies on multi-stage, heavily obfuscated VBScript and PowerShell, self-extracting archives and LNK files, with scheduled tasks for persistence [S1][S2]. Malware includes the Pterodo family, QuietSieve, PowerPunch, DinoTrain, DesertDown, DilongTrash, ObfuBerry and ObfuMerry, plus UltraVNC for interactive access [S1][S2]. ESET documented an expanding set of Ptero-series PowerShell tools, including PteroSand, PteroPaste, PteroOdd, PteroGraphin and PteroSetup, with six new tools in 2025 [S7][S9]. The group spreads through USB and removable drives, which can reach air-gapped machines [S6][S7]. Its infrastructure churns quickly: Microsoft saw more than 25 new domains and more than 80 IPs in a 30-day window, with DNS records changing about daily and mostly hosted on REG.RU [S1]. Unit 42 counted more than 500 new domains over 10 months [S5]. The group has used Telegram and Telegraph dead drops to find C2 addresses [S6]. It has hidden almost all of its C2 behind Cloudflare tunnels (2024) and Cloudflare Workers (from May 2025), and has also used devtunnels.ms, Loophole, No-IP, Clever Cloud, Supabase, Dropbox and S3-compatible storage for exfiltration [S8][S9].

campaigns.name: Operation Armageddon (start)
campaigns.summary: LookingGlass reports spearphishing against Ukrainian government, law enforcement and military officials from at least mid-2013. Attack waves track political events around Ukraine's EU Association Agreement and the conflict.

campaigns.name: Gamaredon toolset evolution
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 names the group, reports a move to custom-developed malware, and documents its use of compromised domains, dynamic DNS and Russian hosting.

campaigns.name: SSU public attribution
campaigns.summary: The SSU names five alleged members, describes them as Crimean FSB officers acting on orders from the FSB Center for Information Security, and claims more than 5,000 cyberattacks on Ukrainian authorities and critical infrastructure.

campaigns.name: State Migration Service of Ukraine phishing
campaigns.summary: Unit 42, as reported by The Hacker News, describes a Word lure against Ukraine's State Migration Service that installed UltraVNC.

campaigns.name: Western government entity in Ukraine
campaigns.summary: A malware downloader disguised as a resume was uploaded to a Ukrainian job-search platform in response to an active job listing for the targeted Western government organization (Unit 42, as reported by The Hacker News).

campaigns.name: Microsoft ACTINIUM disclosure
campaigns.summary: Microsoft describes campaigns since October 2021 against Ukrainian government, military, NGO, judicial, law-enforcement and aid-coordination organizations, using remote-template phishing and the Pterodo and QuietSieve families, among others.

campaigns.name: NATO-state petroleum refinery attempt
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 reports an unsuccessful attempt to compromise a large petroleum refining company in a NATO member state, as part of a period in which it tracked more than 500 new domains and 200 samples.

campaigns.name: Shuckworm intrusions on Ukrainian security and military bodies
campaigns.summary: Symantec, as reported by The Hacker News, describes intrusions beginning in February/March 2023 that lasted up to three months, used USB propagation of Pterodo, located C2 through Telegram and Telegraph, and stole battlefield-related reports.

campaigns.name: Intensified spearphishing against Ukrainian government
campaigns.summary: ESET reports that the group focused exclusively on Ukrainian government institutions, sharply increased spearphishing in the second half of 2024, and hid almost all of its C2 behind Cloudflare tunnels.

campaigns.name: Gamaredon-Turla collaboration
campaigns.summary: ESET observes PteroGraphin restarting Turla's Kazuar on a Ukrainian machine, followed in April and June 2025 by Kazuar v2 deployed through PteroOdd and PteroPaste. ESET detected Turla on seven machines in Ukraine.

campaigns.name: WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 exploitation
campaigns.summary: ESET reports exploitation of CVE-2025-8088 to drop HTA downloaders into the Startup folder. This was part of 35 distinct spearphishing campaigns in 2025 against Ukrainian government and military institutions.

diamond.adversary: Officers of the Russian FSB in Crimea (Center 18), according to the SSU attribution, which Microsoft repeats [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.capability: High-volume spearphishing with remote template injection, HTML smuggling, HTA, VBScript and PowerShell chains; Pterodo/Ptero-series tools, QuietSieve, PowerPunch and UltraVNC; USB propagation; and WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 [S1][S6][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Rapidly rotating domains and IPs, largely on REG.RU [S1][S5]; Telegram and Telegraph dead drops [S6]; Cloudflare tunnels and Workers, devtunnels.ms, Loophole, No-IP, Clever Cloud, Supabase, Dropbox and S3-compatible storage [S8][S9].
diamond.victim: Ukrainian government, military, security-service, judicial, law-enforcement and NGO organizations [S1][S6][S9]. Occasionally Western or NATO-state entities: a Western government body in Ukraine and a NATO-state refinery [S4][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection supporting Russia's war against Ukraine, including information on aid coordination, territorial security and battlefield reporting [S1][S6]. The group may also act as an access broker for Turla [S7].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints with Office, WinRAR and scripting hosts (mshta, wscript, PowerShell); removable media; and trusted cloud and tunnelling services used to blend in with normal traffic [S1][S6][S9].

gaps: Primary vendor reports could not be fetched (Unit 42, ESET WeLiveSecurity and ESET white papers, Symantec, The Record). Details for S4-S9 rely on search-result and press coverage of those reports.
The SSU's original 2021 announcement and its claims (names, more than 5,000 attacks, Center 18 tasking) were not opened directly and are not independently verified [S3].
Microsoft has not published its own confidence level for the FSB attribution; it repeats the Ukrainian government attribution [S1][S2].
The exact date of ESET's 2022-2023 toolset white paper (reported as September 2024) and its NATO-country targeting details were not verified from the primary document [S13].
The full scope and the victims of Gamaredon's non-Ukrainian targeting are unclear. The public cases are few and unnamed [S4][S5].
The division of labour between Gamaredon and Turla is not public beyond ESET's technical observations (for example, whether Gamaredon brokers access as tasked or opportunistically) [S7].
No public reporting was found on Aqua Blizzard targeting US DoD networks directly.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): The key terrain is Ukrainian government and military networks, and the networks of partners who coordinate aid to Ukraine [S1]. Western government and NATO-state entities operating in or supporting Ukraine are secondary terrain [S4][S5]. Removable media can bridge to air-gapped segments [S6]. STEP 2 (effects): Constant domain churn and abuse of trusted cloud and tunnel services such as Cloudflare, Telegram and Dropbox weaken static blocklists and reputation-based filtering [S1][S8][S9]. STEP 3 (adversary template): The chain runs from a spearphish (remote template, HTML smuggling, archive or WinRAR exploit) to an HTA, VBS or PowerShell downloader, then a Ptero-series implant with scheduled-task persistence, then USB spread and document theft. Selected hosts may be handed off to Turla's Kazuar [S1][S6][S7][S9]. STEP 4: The MLCOA is continued mass spearphishing for intelligence on Ukrainian military and government operations [S8][S9]. The MDCOA is access to a coalition or NATO-partner network supporting Ukraine, brokered to a more capable FSB actor (Turla) for long-term espionage [S5][S7]. Candidate indicators: mshta, wscript or PowerShell spawned from Office or WinRAR; new scheduled tasks with wordlist-style names; LNK files appearing on USB drives; and outbound traffic to trycloudflare, workers.dev, devtunnels.ms, Telegraph or Telegram from non-browser processes [S1][S6][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: the actor's tempo (35 campaigns in 2025) and infrastructure churn mean behaviour-based detections must feed JCC2 common operating picture tools, not just IOC feeds [S1][S9]. (2) Authorities: the attribution to the FSB comes from the Ukrainian government and vendors. Microsoft has not given a confidence level, so planners should not present it as a US government attribution without a separate basis [S1][S3]. (3) Mission assurance: units and contractors supporting aid or security cooperation with Ukraine should enforce controls on removable media and Office and WinRAR patching, given the USB propagation and CVE-2025-8088 exploitation [S6][S9]. (4) Coordination: because Gamaredon may hand access to Turla, any Gamaredon detection on partner or coalition networks should trigger a hunt for Kazuar-class follow-on implants and be shared with coalition CERTs [S7].
